title: Greg Sherwood MW: Klein Graniet – small property, serious Stellenbosch Cabernet
summary:
Klein Graniet is a small boutique family wine farm on the R44 highway, on the western slopes of the Simonsberg just a few kilometres north of Stellenbosch. It is a small five-hectare estate that has stayed small on purpose, and its stated belief over the years has been that excellence comes from focusing on quality, […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: Klein Graniet – small property, serious Stellenbosch Cabernet appeared first on winemag.
content:
Klein Graniet is a small boutique family wine farm on the R44 highway, on the western slopes of the Simonsberg just a few kilometres north of Stellenbosch. It is a small five-hectare estate that has stayed small on purpose, and its stated belief over the years has been that excellence comes from focusing on quality, not quantity.

My interest in this small estate was recently reignited after retasting both their Cabernet Sauvignon 2021 and their Tribute Cape Bordeaux Blend 2021 at the Cabernet Collective tasting in London, where both wines greatly impressed me.

Their story is a fairly long one, according to co-proprietor Retief du Toit, with the original farm being bought back in 1998 from the son-in-law of ex-President P.W.Botha, with vines planted on the small property from 2008 onwards, and the first experimental vintages only bottled in 2011.

The estate was originally bought by Marc Wiehe, their stepfather and then owner of the L’Avenir wine estate, and his wife, Hester. It now belongs entirely to the Du Toit family and is farmed by brothers Retief and Stefan, the latter also making the Klein Graniet wines.

The brothers named the estate and its original label Deux Frères, honouring their respective partnership, with the vineyards sitting on traditional Stellenbosch decomposed granite soils. This helped shape their farming philosophy with wines only made from their own vines, carefully farmed with the sole aim being to express the precise character of the farm’s terroir and soils through their wines.

Transition from Deux Frères to Klein Graniet

In 2025 the label required a change. The estate announced the renaming of its wine label from Deux Frères to Klein Graniet, a name reflecting both the geology and the landscape of the property. The name works on two levels, Retief told me, “Klein” being Afrikaans for small, and a nod to the compact nature of the family farm with only four hectares of vines, and “Graniet” referring to the famous Granitic soils of the property.

“This was merely a change of label, not of ownership or place,” Retief confirms, stating that the farm continues today to carry the Deux Frères name, honouring their legacy as brothers, winemakers and stewards of the land. But in the end, the wines required a name change after a serious legal challenge from the Deux Frères craft Gin distillery in Zurich, Switzerland, ultimately forced the decision.

Today, a notable Stellenbosch single cultivar Cabernet Sauvignon anchors the range, the same grape also forming the foundation of their flagship red, the Tribute Cape Bordeaux Blend, which is complemented by additions of Petit Verdot, Malbec and Cabernet Franc.

As always, all the fruit used for Klein Graniet’s wines are estate farmed and grown with the exception of a small parcel of Old Vine Sauvignon Blanc planted in 1985 on the neighbouring farm owned by the Slayley Family Estate but managed and farmed by brothers Retief and Stefan.

This Old Vine Sauvignon Blanc block is one of the three oldest certified Sauvignon Blanc plantings in the Cape, another being the very impressive Les Dames de 1987 block produced by Terre Plaisible in Franschhoek, made by winemaking legend Adam Mason.

Another notable wine in the Klein Graniet range is of course their excellent single cultivar Mourvèdre. Originally produced as a Shiraz / Mourvèdre blend in a handful of vintages, it was eventually decided for commercial as well as quality reasons, to discontinue the Shiraz and regraft the vines to Cabernet Franc, leaving the Mourvèdre red to become its own unique entity.

Alongside the Mourvèdre red, Klein Graniet also produces a very notable Mourvèdre Rosé. A true rarity in the Cape when used in its pure form a la Bandol in France (the other noteworthy Stellenbosch example being the famous Cape Coral Rosé from Waterkloof), Klein Graniet farms a single block of it in deeper, sandy granitic soils with part of the crop consigned to a dry Rosé wine, picked early for freshness and then given a very gentle skin contact that produces its signature pale salmon colour – for me, a real gem in the range.

The Klein Graniet vines might now be settling into their late teenage years, planted at 5,000 to 5,500 vines per hectare density compared to the normal 3,000 to 3,500 vines per hectare average, yielding a healthy eight tons of grapes per hectare on average, nevertheless, the estate retains an element of unwarranted anonymity among many consumers.

Quality considered, the most exciting times seemingly still lie ahead for this small boutique winery that is slowly but surely making steady inroads into the UK’s more discerning fine wine collector market.

In mid-October, I caught up with fellow Pretoria boy Retief du Toit in London for a one-on-one range tasting and chat after showing his wines at the Wines of South Africa ‘There’s Sunshine Inside’ Trade Tasting 2026. My full notes are below.

Klein Graniet Cabernet Sauvignon 2020, WO Stellenbosch, 14% Abv.

Made from three different clones planted in this block with almost solid Granite as the bedrock. Aged in French oak barriques for circa 22 months, the wine shows classical layers of violets and dried herbs, black currant, crushed Granite, sweet cedar oak spice and a hint of black chai tea leaf and graphite. The mouthfeel of fleshy and incredibly supple, showing a peppery, earthy black berry spice, hints of earthy plum and sappy oak with a dusting of Christmas spices. Full and fleshy, this wine speaks of a ripe, warm, muscular vintage for Cabernet Sauvignon. Drink this Cabernet Sauvignon now or age comfortably for another 8 to 10 years.

(93/100 Greg Sherwood MW)

Klein Graniet Tribute Cape Bordeaux Blend 2019, WO Stellenbosch, 14% Abv.

A blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Petit Verdot and Malbec aged for 24 months in 225 litre French barriques with circa 15% new, reveals an aromatics of smoky gunpowder, sweet lavender, violets, wet tobacco leaf and pepper corn spice over lashings of rich earthy black and blue berry fruits, all underpinned by a dusty, crushed Granitic minerality. The palate is sweet fruited and impressively fleshy and elegant, the concentrated blue and black berry fruits delightfully harmonious, the tannins polished and pinpoint and the acids very well integrated contributing to a whole that is bigger than the sum of its parts. An intelligently assembled Cape Bordeaux blend that is drinking very well at the moment but should age effortlessly for another 8 to 10 years.

(94/100 Greg Sherwood MW)

Klein Graniet No 42. Mourvèdre 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 12.5% Abv.

Made from 13-year-old vines, the grapes were fermented in open top fermenters using only gentle pump overs and no punch downs, before being transferred to old 500 litre French barrels for 12 months. The aromatics are beautifully fragrant and lifted boasting complex notes of bramble berries, wild strawberries, macerated oranges, citrus peel and delicately sappy cedar spice notes. Beautifully elegant and light touch, there is plenty of elegance and finesse on display, the fruit obviously handled very sensitively to ensure a fine-grained texture and supple powdery tannins all wrapped in a juicy, tangy acidity. The top notes of black cherry and blue berry spice develop in the glass and linger on a cool, focused finish. Seamless, silky and effortlessly accessible with an underlying structure making it a wonderfully characterful gastronomic wine. Drink now and over the next 5 to 8+ years.

(94+/100 Greg Sherwood MW)

Klein Graniet Mourvèdre Rosé 2025, WO Stellenbosch, 12% Abv.

Made from pure Mourvedre, this pale salmon pink Rosé shares a lot in common with the great wines of Bandol in the South of France. The aromatics reveal a subtle struck flint reduction before hints of red currants, cranberry and potpourri over a solid base of Granitic mineral spice. Vibrant and mouthwatering, the superb 2025 vintage in the Cape offers up a vibrantly energetic palate of orange peel, cranberry and tart red cherry fruits, layered with a wet stone minerality and a gentle dusting of dried herb nuances on the finish. Succulent, tangy but dry on the finish, this is a seriously delicious Rosé to build your summer around! Drink now and over the next 2 to 4+ years.

(93+/100 Greg Sherwood MW)

Klein Graniet Sauvignon Blanc 2024, WO Stellenbosch, 12% Abv.

Sourced from a 1.5-hectare plot of Old Vine Sauvignon Blanc planted in 1985 on the neighbouring Slayley Estate farm that is dryland farmed and tended by Klein Graniet. Stainless steel fermented but left on its lees for 4 months, it shows impressively pure, crystalline notes of white peach, green melon, Cape Gooseberry and freshly cut Granny Smith apples with a delicate undertone of Granitic mineral complexity. Fleshy and supple in the mouth, there is a cool, glycerol weight to the wine, hints of yellow orchard fruits, quince and more green apple notes, leading to a long, tangy classically dry finish. Drink now to 2030+.

(92+/100 Greg Sherwood MW)

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

title: FermTech briefing: 2027 vintage – don’t predict, prepare
summary:
Every wine vintage brings its own opportunities and challenges. Yet perhaps the greatest risk for winemakers is assuming we know what those challenges will be before the growing season has fully unfolded. As South Africa approaches the 2027 harvest, there are a few climatic conditions worth taking a closer look at. Winter rainfall, accumulated chill, […]

The post FermTech briefing: 2027 vintage – don’t predict, prepare appeared first on winemag.
content:
Every wine vintage brings its own opportunities and challenges. Yet perhaps the greatest risk for winemakers is assuming we know what those challenges will be before the growing season has fully unfolded.

As South Africa approaches the 2027 harvest, there are a few climatic conditions worth taking a closer look at. Winter rainfall, accumulated chill, early budburst and regional water availability give us a better understanding of where our vineyards stand as we head into the growing season.

This does not mean we can predict the vintage. What it does mean is that we can identify some of the risks early and start preparing for them.

At FermTech Solutions, our approach is straightforward: understand what we know, consider what might develop, and prepare for what we can control.

Understanding the conditions entering 2027

The period preceding the 2027 growing season has presented a combination of encouraging developments and potential vulnerabilities.

Beneficial rainfall during April and May 2026 supported vineyard recovery and reserve replenishment ahead of winter dormancy. This was followed by relatively warm and dry winter conditions across several wine-producing regions.

Despite warmer temperatures, available assessments indicated that most regions accumulated sufficient winter chill to support budburst. However, warmer August conditions contributed to budburst occurring approximately two to three weeks earlier than usual in certain areas.

September rainfall and favourable storage levels in several major irrigation dams provided further reassurance regarding regional water availability.

Similarly, adequate regional chill accumulation does not guarantee uniform budburst across every cultivar or vineyard block, which is clear in some Chardonnay vineyards in the Franschhoek Valley.

Early budburst: opportunity or vulnerability?

Earlier budburst is one of the more significant observations entering the 2027 season.

One potential consequence is a growing disconnect between sugar accumulation and phenolic maturity.

Under elevated temperatures or increasing water stress, grapes may accumulate sugar before achieving the desired flavour and tannin development. Winemakers could therefore face difficult harvesting decisions: pick at the preferred sugar concentration with less-developed phenolics, or delay harvesting while risking higher alcohol, declining acidity and possible fruit deterioration.

Changes in berry size and skin-to-pulp ratio may also influence extraction behaviour, colour concentration and tannin balance.

These outcomes remain possibilities rather than predictions, but they warrant consideration when preparing for the coming harvest.

Preparing for different vintage scenarios

Rather than forecasting a particular outcome, FermTech has identified three plausible scenarios.

A favourable vintage would feature adequate water availability, moderate temperatures, healthy fruit and progressive ripening. Under these conditions, cellar decisions can concentrate on precision, varietal expression and stylistic objectives.

A heat- and water-constrained vintage could produce elevated sugar concentrations, altered acidity, variable phenolic maturity and changes in yeast-assimilable nitrogen. Such conditions would place greater emphasis on fermentation planning and nutritional management.

A variable or disruptive vintage could involve late-season rainfall, disease pressure, severe heat events or wildfire smoke exposure. These conditions may introduce uneven maturity, microbial pressure, oxidation susceptibility and compromised fruit quality.

Importantly, these scenarios are not mutually exclusive. Different regions, cultivars and individual vineyards may experience contrasting conditions during the same season.

The objective is therefore not to prepare for one anticipated outcome, but to develop the technical flexibility to respond appropriately.

Understanding must composition

One of the most important principles in winemaking is that the vintage influences grape composition, but measured grape composition should determine the fermentation protocol.

Sugar concentration, pH, total acidity, malic acid, yeast-assimilable nitrogen (YAN), glucose-to-fructose ratio, turbidity and fruit health provide the analytical foundation for effective fermentation management.

As a winemaker, I have always believed that prevention is better than cure. If we understand the composition of our must from the outset, we have an opportunity to address potential problems early, before they carry through into the finished wine.

Elevated sugar concentrations increase potential alcohol and can place additional physiological demands on yeast. Inadequate or imbalanced nitrogen availability may further compromise fermentation performance, increasing the likelihood of sluggish or incomplete fermentations.

Yeast selection and nutrition therefore become important tools for managing vintage-related fermentation risk. This is especially true in dryland vineyards, whereby insufficient Winter rainfall and soil moisture can disrupt nutrient mobility, and therefore reduced nitrogen assimilation to the grapes.

FermTech’s VitiFerm BIO organic yeast portfolio provides strain-selection options suited to different fermentation objectives. FermControl BIO offers an organic nutrition approach incorporating amino-acid-based nitrogen, micronutrients and vitamins to support yeast metabolism.

The intention is not routine supplementation, but targeted nutritional management based on the actual requirements of the must.

Managing compromised fruit and oxidation

Vintage conditions can also influence the oxidative susceptibility of grapes, juice and wine.

Fruit condition, phenolic composition, press fractions and oxygen exposure all affect oxidation chemistry and its potential consequences for aroma, colour and palate structure.

Compromised fruit introduces additional challenges, particularly where rot, disease pressure or smoke exposure affects grape quality.

ClearUP BIO provides a treatment option for certain undesirable compounds associated with compromised fruit, including specific rot-related and smoke-taint applications, where appropriate analysis and validated protocols support its use.

Reprise BIO offers an additional approach to antioxidant protection and phenolic harmonisation, particularly where preservation of fruit expression and freshness is a priority.

These interventions should be selected according to the identified problem rather than applied indiscriminately.

Microbial management in higher-risk wines

Elevated grape and wine pH deserves particular attention because it reduces the antimicrobial effectiveness of sulphur dioxide and increases susceptibility to unwanted microbial activity.

Malolactic fermentation (MLF) is therefore more than a process of converting malic acid into lactic acid. It is also an important microbial management decision.

Certain indigenous Pediococcus and Lactobacillus strains can conduct MLF but may possess undesirable metabolic pathways associated with volatile acidity, biogenic amines or other spoilage characteristics.

Selecting an appropriate MaloBacti culture encourages controlled MLF and reduces reliance on unpredictable indigenous bacterial populations.

Strain selection can also influence wine style. MaloBacti CN1 provides a citrate-negative option where avoiding citrate-derived diacetyl formation is desirable. Comparative trials with MaloBacti HF2 have demonstrated lower β-glucosidase activity and improved anthocyanin retention relative to the bacterial strains tested, suggesting potential benefits for red wine colour preservation.

Preserving phenolic architecture

Vintage conditions can influence tannin development, anthocyanin concentration, extraction behaviour and the eventual balance between fruit expression, colour and palate structure.

These considerations become particularly relevant when grapes enter the cellar with uneven phenolic maturity or altered skin-to-pulp ratios.

The ViniTannin portfolio, including SR, Supreme and Multi Extra, provides options for targeted colour and phenolic management.

The objective is not simply to increase tannin concentration, but to identify specific structural vulnerabilities and select interventions that support colour stability, phenolic integration and the intended wine style.

Ultimately, effective phenolic management should preserve the identity of the vineyard rather than impose a uniform character on the wine.

Preparedness rather than prediction

The 2027 vintage will be shaped by climatic conditions that have yet to unfold.

What winemakers can control is their preparedness.

By monitoring vineyard development, understanding grape composition and anticipating potential fermentation, oxidative, microbial and phenolic challenges, we can make more informed decisions as the season progresses.

At FermTech Solutions, our role is to translate these insights into practical cellar strategies, supported by appropriate technical products, analytical interpretation and application-specific protocols.

The opportunity for 2027 is not to predict the vintage correctly, but to be sufficiently prepared to respond intelligently, whatever the vintage delivers.

  • Clayton Reabow owns FermTech Solutions, the South African distributor of 2B FermControl – a range of organic fermentation products for minimal-intervention winemaking. With more than 22 years’ experience in the local wine industry, Reabow combines winemaking expertise with a practical understanding of supply chains and production. His goal is to help producers maintain quality while staying efficient and competitive in a changing market.

title: Jamie Goode: Does how a wine is made matter more than how it tastes?
summary:
Imagine you run a factory. Say you are making cars. There are two approaches to ensuring that your cars reach the market in a functional way, and with the sort of quality that you expect. [And, an aside, I was a child in the 1970s UK, and was quite obsessed by cars. Many of the […]

The post Jamie Goode: Does how a wine is made matter more than how it tastes? appeared first on winemag.
content:
Imagine you run a factory. Say you are making cars. There are two approaches to ensuring that your cars reach the market in a functional way, and with the sort of quality that you expect. [And, an aside, I was a child in the 1970s UK, and was quite obsessed by cars. Many of the famous brands were being made by a state-owned conglomerate called British Leyland, and the quality of these cars was regarded as terrible. British car manufacturers were really bad at that time, and when the Germans bought the Mini brand, they were astonished by how wide the tolerances were in UK car manufacturing.]

Process versus quality control

One approach is process based. Make sure that the process is so accurate and the attention to detail is spot on, and then the cars that roll off the production line should be fine. The other is to rely on quality control at the other end. You know that some of the cars won’t be great, so you test everything carefully post-manufacture, and stop the duds (the ‘Friday afternoon cars’) from reaching the market. Of course, most factories will use a mixture of the two approaches.

It’s a bit like this with making wine. Is your philosophy to be super-technical and in control of the whole production process, or are you going to be less interventionist, leave a bit to chance, and then hope to have some robust quality control at the end?

This is all about the issue of agency, and I think this is where we see a big philosophical divide in wine.

As a winemaker, are you making wine? Or is your role more of that of a custodian, where you choose your vineyard and your method of élevage to match, but where your philosophy is that you are allowing a wine to be formed and your role merely to guide it to the place where it ends up?

This leads us to the question that’s the title of this piece. Does the production philosophy matter more than the flavour? Outspoken biodynamic pioneer Nicolas Joly sums this up in his famous phrase, ‘Before being good, a wine should be true.’ For Joly, if a wine is not ‘true’, and we can debate what he means by this, it doesn’t matter how nice it tastes, it is illegitimate and so how it tastes is a moot point.

Truth versus taste

At one extreme, this position is a sound one. Say I make a wine, and you add things to it (such as sugar and flavourings) and then a group of tasters is presented the pair of wines and prefers the adulterated one. To them, this wine tastes better. But I don’t care about this, because it is an illegal, illegitimate, untrue wine. Legally, this wine is not true.

Someone like Joly might argue that if a wine is made from conventionally farmed grapes, where some herbicide and systemic fungicide have been used, then this wine is not true. They might have a list of winery operations (such as filtration or fining) that make a wine untrue. I wouldn’t go as far as this, but I understand the perspective.

For some people, production philosophy matters more than flavour. This is found in the natural wine movement, where some take a hardline zero-zero position, and won’t even contemplate adding sulfites at bottling. Some wines lose quality because of this approach, in the sense that to a normal taster, they don’t taste as good as they might have done had some sulfites had been added. There are some natural wines with above threshold levels of 4EP and 4EG (from Brettanomyces) or elevated volatile acidity levels, and there will be natural wine lovers who would rather encounter these characters in the wine than contemplate protective additions of sulfites. They are entirely within their rights in doing this, but it’s a situation where the production philosophy has come before flavour in decision making. I’ve even heard some argue that we should put up with a bit of mousiness and not hold natural winegrowers to the same standard we might hold other winemakers, because they are taking more risks.

On the other hand there are winemakers who hold to very tight production standards, because they want to make clean wines, and don’t want to risk any faults. Of course, if you are working for a large winery, your route to market might demand clean, consistent wines and there may be no tolerance for variation. Here we come back to the issue of taste. Whereas the consumers who go to natural wine bars have some tolerance for varying flavours, supermarket shoppers probably have less tolerance. I haven’t got firm data on this, but my impression from many years of going to press tastings suggest that crisp, focused, fruit-driven wines are valued in this market channel. And to reliably make wines like this at scale requires a process-based view where winemaking steps can ensure consistency and cleanliness even with some variation in the fruit that they receive. For supermarket customers taste is primary.

When it comes to low-intervention/natural wines, I’m not saying taste doesn’t matter. It’s just that production philosophy is primary. Hopefully, a natural production philosophy results in a wine that is true to place and which tastes better, but the most important thing is that the wine is an honest one. When I visit a wine bar specializing in interesting wine, whether or not it is a natural wine bar, I’m seeking authenticity. I come to learn. I want to taste a wine that comes from somewhere, and which is a product of a microbiological process. I want to like it, but sometimes I need to admire it first for what it is, and then learn to like it. I don’t need the immediate hedonic hit, and I won’t trade that for authenticity.

So, yes, production philosophy and ideology sometimes come first, and I think they should. Everyone has their line in the sand; for all of us there is a level of intervention, whether in the vineyard or the winery, which we are uncomfortable going beyond in our drinking. And sometimes the line in the sand moves according to drinking occasion and budget. I think this is entirely legitimate, even though I won’t join the zero-zero folks and their purity tests. There are some simple interventions that can stop a wine being irredeemably spoiled, and in this case, please do intervene rather than present me a wine with mouse or a VA of 1.7 g/litre!

  • Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.

title: Tim James: Obscure and mostly moribund grape crosses in Cape vineyards
summary:
I was pleased to see Malu Lambert report, in her piece on palomino, that Adi Badenhorst is “propagating” colomino, a local cross of palomino and colombar. It seems to have been a largely unappreciated variety since some boffin in a lab had thought it a good idea and sent it through all the hoops to […]

The post Tim James: Obscure and mostly moribund grape crosses in Cape vineyards appeared first on winemag.
content:
I was pleased to see Malu Lambert report, in her piece on palomino, that Adi Badenhorst is “propagating” colomino, a local cross of palomino and colombar. It seems to have been a largely unappreciated variety since some boffin in a lab had thought it a good idea and sent it through all the hoops to get to market. Perhaps it will still prove to have been a good idea. But I had once, looking at the changing shape of the Cape vineyard this century, wistfully hoped Adi would take up the claims of an equally obscure cross called brakboseiland, which I think would somehow have better suited his beard and sense of humour. Incidentally, there appears to be a pretty nondescript geographical feature in the Northern Cape with this name, presumably with some connection to the grape.

Unfortunately, however, brakboseiland has disappeared from the list of permitted vine cultivars, as per the latest update of the Wine of Origin Scheme. Actually, colomino is not there either, so, according to my understanding, Adi couldn’t sell any wine under that name until it’s reinstated. If I look at the list of plantings for 2010, I see that Brakboseiland had no plantings recorded, while there had been 0.75 hectares of the stuff ten years earlier. And colomino was moving in the same direction: 4.58 ha in 2010, down from 16.03. A further decline left only 0.03 ha in 2025 (I wonder if those are Adi’s vines?).

The vanishing crosses

Looking through those lists of vinifera grape varieties, one is struck by the number of the more obscure names that refer to deliberate grape crosses – that is, varieties intentionally created by the wine industry, rather than having emerged and been selected over centuries of “natural”, spontaneous life in the vineyards. The aim of such crosses is to combine different characteristics, frequently high quality and high productivity, but also resistance to temperature and disease. (NB, these are not hybrids – that term refers to crosses between different species, with an offspring that is, in this case, not part of the vinifera species.)

Some in the list refer to crosses created elsewhere – ruby cabernet, for example, which was bred in California from cabernet sauvignon (for quality) and carignan (productivity and heat tolerance), and is still the ninth-most-planted variety here. But most crosses on the list (and increasingly falling off it, it seems) are local creations. By far the best known, of course, is pinotage, which is locally and internationally unusual for being a cross that is widely regarded as a grape that can and does produce high-quality wine. And also for being so successful, comfortably in the top half-dozen plantings here and generally on the up, rather than the down.

Decline is a far more common story for even the most successful of deliberate crosses: Müller-Thurgau, bred at Geisenheim Grape Breeding Institute in Germany in the late 19th century from riesling and madeleine royale (though it took later DNA research to ascertain madeleine’s role), has been widely and intensively planted round the world to cover great areas (but never tried here as far as I know), although hectarage was markedly in decline in recent decades.

After pinotage, the highest place for a local cross on our list is nouvelle, jogging along at around 360 ha. Bred from crouchen and ugni blanc by Chris Orffer (our preeminent grape breeder, who clearly enjoyed the process), it dates back some 60 years, but took off in a small way this century. In 2000 there was less than 2 ha of it, but someone no doubt recalled that it could contribute some extra pyrazenes and grassiness to sauvignon blanc, qualities rather more admired then than now. Nouvelle has that character in a big way. I doubt if it ever appears in anything other than a blend.

The local crossing that comes next in terms of plantings is roobernet, from cabernet sauvignon and alicante bouschet (the latter itself a French cross), again by Orffer. A fascinating and instructive story about this was recently told on Wine Goggle by Emile Joubert, who discusses the significance of its being the same crossing as the earlier Odesa Black, bred in the Ukraine. It’s a good story (though perhaps Emile and I are both unusually eccentric in finding these minor bits of local wine history fascinating); but I think he’s wrong in concluding that these two are “the same cultivar” and that ruby cab is “not a Stellenbosch invention”. All these crosses involve sexual, not vegetative, reproduction, and crossing the same parents will result in offspring at least as different as human siblings are from one another, and just as worthy of different names. Ruby cab deserves its place on the list – while it’s there, as it is a fading presence, albeit still robust. And it undoubtedly should have been included in the great Jancis Robinson et al book on Wine Grapes, which it is not.

The also-rans of the breeding programme

As to the few other local crossings which linger on but are essentially moribund, there’s nothing much to say, except (seeing as I’m here) to mention them dutifully. Chenel (chenin and ugni blanc, the last bit of its name recalling Elsenburg) was once widely planted but there’s little of it left. Grachen (more pyrozenes, reportedy; I notice the name is more or less an anagram of grenache, but I have no idea if that’s relevant) seems to have been one of the later Orffer offerings, but I’d never even heard of it till perusing these lists. Weldra (Welgevallen + dra (carry/bear)) is another chenin-ugni blanc cross, bred to provide high yields for the brandy industry but clearly in even more dire straits than brandy. Neither of these two made it to Robinson’s Wine Grapes, which seems wrong but not worth making a fuss about as they’re almost dead – though, strangely, at least weldra did appear in Jancis’s much earlier Guide to Wine Grapes.

Good luck to Badenhorst-revived colomino, though my hopes are of the faintest. I do still want to hear more about mysterious brakboseiland, and hope that what appears to be its passing (without ever having been properly noticed!) might not be the case.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

The post Recipe: Goulash soup with spinach and peas appeared first on winemag.
content:
Serve with Lanzerac Pionier Pinotage 2014.

Hungry? Hungary has the answer.

Serves 4

Ingredients:
2 tbsp (30ml) olive oil
2 onions, finely chopped
2 carrots, peeled and roughly chopped
2 celery sticks, finely sliced
2 cloves of garlic, crushed
1 tbsp (15ml) paprika
600g beef goulash, cubed
salt and freshly ground pepper
pinch of dried chilli flakes (optional)
1 tbsp (15ml) tomato paste
1 tin chopped tomatoes
1l beef stock
2 potatoes, peeled and cubed
½ cup (125ml) frozen peas
150g baby spinach
crusty bread to serve

Method:
Heat olive oil in a heavy based pot and sauté onions, carrots, celery and garlic for a few minutes until lightly golden brown.

Add paprika and goulash and brown well.

Season with salt and freshly ground pepper, add chilli and stir in the tomato paste.

Add chopped tomatoes and beef stock and cook over a low heat for 1½ – 2 hours or until the meat is tender.

Add potatoes and cook for a further 15-20 minutes or until almost cooked through.

Add peas and spinach and cook for a couple more minutes or until peas have softened and spinach has wilted.

Check seasoning and serve immediately with crusty bread.

Wine pairing:
A robust, earthy wine is required to stand up to the strong flavours of the dish – try a Pinotage or full-bodied Shiraz.
